items.question_text: A 46-year-old man attends a Darwin general practice for a repeat script. He mentions that his mother was Aboriginal. He has not had a health assessment. He is well, works, and has no chronic disease recorded. A colleague says a 715 cannot be offered unless he has a certificate or looks Aboriginal. Eligibility for a 715 is by self-identification, not appearance, and not more often than every 9 months. He identifies when asked. He should be offered the assessment. What is the most appropriate action?  He has capacity and agrees when the question is put properly. There is no 715 in the last 9 months. Offer it. Appearance and a missing certificate are not the test.  He has lived in the city for years and was never asked at previous clinics. Blood pressure today is normal. There is no recent complete check. The 715 is an offer, not a test of appearance. Ask, and if he identifies, offer it.  No certificate is required. Self-identification is enough. Offer the 715 and explain what it covers. Do not wait for him to look a certain way.  Explain the check covers heart risk, diabetes, kidney, and ears as relevant. He can decline. The offer itself is the correct step once he has identified.  He is due. Offer it. Self-identification is the eligibility test. Nothing else is required before the offer.  He agrees to the check once it is explained. Book it.
options: Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification
Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility
Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion
Offer it only if she already has diabetes
Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months
items.subtopic: A 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification, not on appearance, and not more often than every 9 months.
items.explanation:
Item 715 is for a patient of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent, based on self-identification, at any age, in the community. Appearance, city residence, and the absence of a chronic disease do not decide it. It cannot be claimed if the same assessment was done in the preceding 9 months.

A. Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification
She identifies, has Medicare, and has not had one.

B. Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility
There is no urban exclusion.

C. Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion
A certificate is not the Medicare test.

D. Offer it only if she already has diabetes
The assessment is preventive, not limited to known disease.

E. Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months
The claiming interval is 9 months, and she has never had one.
items.diagnosis_explanation: She can be offered a 715 now. Looking Aboriginal, living remotely, or already having a chronic disease is not the rule.
key_takeaways: 715 eligibility is self-identification plus Medicare, any age, in the community.
The claiming interval is 9 months.

items.question_text: A 52-year-old Aboriginal woman asks for help with the cost of her PBS medicines. She has not been registered for Closing the Gap. She asks if she can register herself online. Closing the Gap PBS co-payment registration is a one-off clinical registration by a PBS prescriber or an eligible practitioner. The patient cannot self-register. Register her properly. What is the most appropriate action?  She is eligible once registered. Self-registration is not a pathway. Complete the clinical registration, then her scripts can be annotated. Until then the lower co-payment does not apply.  She has several PBS medicines and is paying the general co-payment. Registration is clinical and one-off. After it is done, annotation works. Before it, writing CTG does nothing. She cannot do this herself online.  Complete the registration in the consult. Explain it is once. After that, CTG annotation is valid. Online self-registration is not a real option.  Do the registration before she leaves. A later phone call often never happens. Eligibility starts at registration, not at the pharmacy counter.  Clinical registration, then she benefits. Self-service online is a myth here. Do it in the room.  Do the registration before the script is reprinted.
options: He can self-register on the Services Australia app
A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment
Registration is only available in remote clinics
He must already be on a concession card
Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy
items.subtopic: Closing the Gap PBS registration is a one-off clinical registration. The patient cannot self-register.
items.explanation:
CTG PBS registration is done once, for life, by a PBS prescriber or an eligible Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner, through HPOS. The patient cannot self-register. It is not limited to remote areas or to concession-card holders, and it follows him across pharmacies.

A. He can self-register on the Services Australia app
Patients cannot self-register.

B. A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment
This is the pathway, and his cost barrier is the clinical point.

C. Registration is only available in remote clinics
Location does not restrict it.

D. He must already be on a concession card
A concession card changes what he pays. It is not the entry rule.

E. Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy
One registration follows him.
items.diagnosis_explanation: He needs a one-off clinical registration. He cannot sign himself up, and he does not need to live remotely.
key_takeaways: CTG PBS registration is one-off, by a prescriber or eligible health practitioner.
It is not limited to remote areas or concession-card holders.

items.question_text: A 12-year-old boy in a remote clinic had acute rheumatic fever last year and is on secondary prophylaxis. His benzathine dose is due. A locum suggests oral penicillin for a week because the clinic is busy. Secondary prophylaxis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, usually every 28 days. An oral course does not replace it. Give the injection. What is the most appropriate action?  He is due, not early. The 28-day interval is the program. Oral penicillin for convenience fails secondary prophylaxis. Give benzathine today.  He had definite acute rheumatic fever. Prophylaxis is current and due today. Busy clinic is not a reason to substitute oral penicillin. Benzathine every 28 days is the regimen. Give it.  Document the dose and the next due date. Oral substitution breaks the prophylaxis that prevents recurrence. Injection today.  Pain of the injection is real. It is not a reason to switch to oral. Give benzathine, record it, book day 28.  Due dose, correct drug, correct route. Oral is not secondary prophylaxis. Inject.  Next dose in 28 days from today. Record both.
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line
Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled
Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose
Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative
One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months
items.subtopic: Secondary prophylaxis after acute rheumatic fever is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, usually every 28 days.
items.explanation:
Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is first-line secondary prophylaxis, given no later than 28 days after the last dose. A 21-day interval is for breakthrough recurrence, not the routine start. Oral penicillin is less effective and is not the routine substitute. Erythromycin is for true penicillin hypersensitivity.

A. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line
Short oral courses are not secondary prophylaxis.

B. Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled
The point of prophylaxis is to prevent the next episode.

C. Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose
This is the guideline regimen.

D. Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative
Macrolide is for hypersensitivity, which she does not have.

E. One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months
The interval is 28 days, not a year.
items.diagnosis_explanation: She needs benzathine benzylpenicillin on a 28-day clock. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days a month is not secondary prophylaxis.
key_takeaways: First-line secondary prophylaxis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.
The routine interval is no later than 28 days.

items.question_text: A 9-year-old in Townsville has fever, migratory arthritis, and a new murmur. You suspect acute rheumatic fever. A colleague says to wait for echocardiogram confirmation before notifying. Acute rheumatic fever is notifiable on clinical suspicion and is registered with the jurisdictional RHD control program. Notify now and link him to the program. What is the most appropriate action?  Jones criteria can be met clinically. Echo will refine carditis but is not a gate for notification. Notify and register now.  Fever, migratory arthritis, and a new murmur in a child in northern Australia is acute rheumatic fever until proved otherwise. Notification is clinical. Echo refines the heart finding. Do not wait for it to notify.  Register with the RHD control program the same day. Echo can be arranged in parallel. Notification does not wait.  Phone the notification. Send the details the program needs. Echo appointment in parallel. Waiting for a scan delays the register.  Clinical notification, program registration, echo in parallel. That is the order.  Clinical suspicion is enough to notify. Do not wait for echo.
options: Notification is only required if he has severe carditis
Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram
Notification is the family's responsibility
Notify now and link him to the RHD control program
Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat
items.subtopic: Acute rheumatic fever is notifiable and is registered with the jurisdictional control program.
items.explanation:
Acute rheumatic fever is notifiable and the child should be registered with the jurisdictional RHD control program. The echocardiogram grades cardiac involvement. It does not gate the notification.

D. Notify now and link him to the RHD control program
Diagnosis is enough.

A. Notification is only required if he has severe carditis
Severity changes prophylaxis duration, not whether he is notified.

B. Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram
That loses the start of secondary prophylaxis and contact care.

C. Notification is the family's responsibility
It is a clinician and public-health duty.

E. Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat
The case is notifiable regardless of contacts.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Definite acute rheumatic fever is notified now. The 6-week echocardiogram does not delay that.
key_takeaways: ARF is notifiable on diagnosis.
Register with the RHD control program at the same time.

items.question_text: A 15-year-old girl had acute rheumatic fever with moderate carditis three years ago. She has had no recurrence. Her mother asks if the benzathine can stop at five years for everyone. Duration of secondary prophylaxis depends on cardiac involvement. Moderate RHD means a longer course than a fixed five years. Continue according to the cardiac category. What is the most appropriate advice?  Moderate carditis lengthens prophylaxis. A blanket five-year stop under-treats her. Follow the RHD duration table, not a fixed course.  Moderate RHD at diagnosis sets a longer duration. Three quiet years do not reset her to a five-year course. Check the category and continue. Stopping early is the error.  Look up the duration for moderate RHD. It is longer than five years. Continue. Do not stop because a parent asked for a fixed end date.  Moderate disease at the start is the category that counts. Quiet years are good. They do not shorten the table. Continue prophylaxis.  Category is moderate. Duration follows category. Five years is not universal. Continue.  The duration table, not a family preference, sets the stop date.
options: Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule
Stop now because adherence has been perfect
Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years
Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram
Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule
items.subtopic: Duration of secondary prophylaxis depends on cardiac involvement, not on a fixed 5-year course for everyone.
items.explanation:
No-carditis disease is a minimum of 5 years or until 21, whichever is longer. Moderate RHD is a minimum of 10 years after the last ARF or until 35, whichever is longer. His cousin's rule does not apply to his valve.

A. Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule
Five years is the no-carditis line.

E. Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule
Moderate disease sets a longer minimum.

B. Stop now because adherence has been perfect
Adherence is why it works. It is not a reason to stop early.

C. Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years
Oral is not the routine remaining regimen.

D. Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram
The family is part of the plan. The duration is clinical.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Moderate RHD does not stop at the no-carditis interval. His cousin's 5-year rule is the wrong line.
key_takeaways: Prophylaxis duration follows cardiac severity.
No carditis is 5 years or age 21. Moderate disease is longer.

items.question_text: An 8-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has infected skin sores and tea-coloured urine. A colleague treats the sores and says no further action is needed. Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is looked for and notified where required. Assess and treat for APSGN. What is the most appropriate action?  Tea-coloured urine after sores is APSGN until proved otherwise. Check blood pressure, urine, and renal function. Notify where required. Do not stop at the skin.  Infected sores plus dark urine in a remote child is APSGN until excluded. Blood pressure may be raised. Oedema may follow. Treat the skin and assess the kidneys. Notify if required.  Check oedema, blood pressure, and urine. Treat sores. Consider notification. APSGN is the diagnosis to chase, not a skin-only problem.  Remote community, sores, dark urine. APSGN pathway: assess, treat skin, notify if the jurisdiction requires. Do not close at topical care.  Sores plus dark urine. APSGN assessment and skin treatment. Notify if required. Do not stop at cream.  Dark urine after sores is not a skin-only visit.
options: Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify
Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks
Give topical mupirocin only
Start frusemide and send him home without bloods
APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis
items.subtopic: Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, and APSGN is looked for and notified where required.
items.explanation:
In northern and remote Australia, APSGN usually follows group A streptococcal skin infection. Oedema, dark urine, and hypertension in a child with sores is APSGN until assessed otherwise. It is notifiable in several jurisdictions and needs same-day clinical care, not a 2-week wait.

B. Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks
The renal signs are the emergency, not the crusts alone.

A. Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify
This is the clinical and public-health move.

C. Give topical mupirocin only
Topical care does not treat APSGN.

D. Start frusemide and send him home without bloods
He needs assessment, not an unmonitored diuretic.

E. APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis
In this setting skin is the usual source.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Puffy eyes, dark urine, and hypertension after skin sores is APSGN until proved otherwise. Do not wait 2 weeks.
key_takeaways: APSGN in remote Australia usually follows skin infection.
Notify and assess the same day.

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man from a Strongyloides-endemic northern community is about to start prednisolone for a flare of asthma. A colleague says to start the steroid and check serology later if he gets abdominal pain. Before steroids in a person from an endemic community, screen or treat for Strongyloides. Do not start steroids alone. What is the most appropriate action?  Steroids can precipitate severe strongyloidiasis. Serology or pre-emptive ivermectin comes first in an endemic-community patient. Starting prednisolone alone is the error.  He grew up in a community where Strongyloides is endemic. Prednisolone without cover risks hyperinfection. Serology or ivermectin first. Then the steroid. Do not reverse that order.  Ivermectin or a negative serology plan before the first steroid dose. Hyperinfection is the risk you are avoiding. Do not start and test later.  Endemic exposure is enough to act before steroids. Do not wait for eosinophilia or abdominal pain. Prevent hyperinfection.  Endemic community, steroids planned. Strongyloides cover or serology first. Then prednisolone.  Endemic exposure plus planned steroids is the trigger to act first.
options: Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression
Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him
Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers
Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely
items.subtopic: Before steroids in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic community, screen or treat. Do not start steroids alone.
items.explanation:
Strongyloides is endemic in many remote northern communities. A normal eosinophil count does not exclude it, and stool microscopy is insensitive. Before immunosuppression he needs serology or pre-emptive ivermectin, because disseminated disease on steroids is dangerous.

A. Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Eosinophilia is often absent.

B. Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression
This is the protective step.

C. Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him
Stool microscopy misses most infections.

D. Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers
Northern Australian communities are endemic.

E. Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely
Remote residence is the reason to consider it.
items.diagnosis_explanation: A normal eosinophil count does not clear Strongyloides. Screen or give ivermectin before the steroids.
key_takeaways: Strongyloides is endemic in remote northern Australia.
Eosinophilia is not required for the diagnosis.

items.question_text: A 48-year-old man in Darwin presents in the wet season with severe pneumonia and sepsis. He works outdoors. Standard community pneumonia antibiotics have been started. He is deteriorating. Melioidosis is treated with ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia cover. Change antibiotics and discuss melioidosis. What is the most appropriate action?  Wet season, outdoor work, severe pneumonia not responding to standard cover. Melioidosis is the concern. Ceftazidime or meropenem, and discuss it. Do not persist with community antibiotics.  Wet-season sepsis and pneumonia in the Top End raises melioidosis. Standard amoxicillin or ceftriaxone alone is not reliable cover. Switch to ceftazidime or meropenem and involve infectious diseases.  Blood cultures first if not done. Then ceftazidime or meropenem. Mention melioidosis in the referral. Community pneumonia treatment has failed.  Top End, wet season, severe pneumonia. Melioidosis until proved otherwise in this picture. Right antibiotic now.  Melioidosis antibiotics now. Ceftazidime or meropenem. Discuss the diagnosis. Do not persist with failed cover.  Wet-season sepsis in the Top End is melioidosis until proved otherwise.
options: Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it
Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis
Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy
Wait for culture before changing antibiotics
items.subtopic: Melioidosis in the tropical wet season is treated with ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia antibiotics.
items.explanation:
Burkholderia pseudomallei is endemic in northern Australia, peaks in the wet season, and prefers people with diabetes. It is resistant to ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Intensive therapy is intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem. Waiting for culture in septic shock is the wrong delay.

A. Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it
It does not.

B. Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis
The organism is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin.

C. Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis
This is the intensive-phase cover.

D. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy
Oral therapy is the eradication phase, not the septic start.

E. Wait for culture before changing antibiotics
Septic shock in this setting is treated on suspicion.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Wet-season pneumonia and shock in a diabetic man in Darwin is melioidosis until proved otherwise. Use ceftazidime or meropenem.
key_takeaways: Melioidosis peaks in the northern wet season and in people with diabetes.
Ceftriaxone and gentamicin do not treat it.

Ask in private. Record what she says. Do not infer from appearance or address. The receptionist’s mark is not an answer.  The question is simple and private. Do not guess from skin, name, or suburb. Record her answer. That answer, not the reception note, drives eligibility for programs.  Correct the record if she identifies. Programs and checks depend on that answer. Appearance is irrelevant.  Private question, direct answer, correct the file. That is the whole task. Inference is the error.  Ask. Record. Do not infer. The receptionist’s assumption is void.  Ask in private and correct the record from her answer. The decision can be made on what is already in the history.

This is the correct practice.

Appearance is not the test.

The clinic asks. It does not wait.

items.question_text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman with known rheumatic heart disease is booked for routine low-risk antenatal care at the local clinic. She has moderate mitral stenosis. A pregnant woman with known RHD needs specialist obstetric and cardiac care, not routine low-risk care alone. Refer and restart prophylaxis if it has lapsed. What is the most appropriate action?  Moderate mitral stenosis in pregnancy is not low-risk antenatal care. She needs obstetric and cardiac specialist input, and prophylaxis must be current. Refer.  Known RHD with mitral stenosis. Pregnancy increases risk. Routine midwife-only care is not enough. Specialist obstetric and cardiac review, and secure prophylaxis, are the plan.  Restart benzathine if the interval has slipped. Book specialist care this week, not at the next routine antenatal visit.  Stenosis plus pregnancy is specialist care. Low-risk booking is wrong. Change the pathway today.  Specialist obstetric and cardiac care. Secure prophylaxis. Not low-risk clinic alone.  Change the booking from low-risk to specialist care today. The decision can be made on what is already in the history.
options: Routine shared care is enough because she feels well
Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy
Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive
RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago
Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis
items.subtopic: A pregnant woman with known RHD needs specialist obstetric and cardiac care, not routine low-risk antenatal care alone.
items.explanation:
Pregnancy increases cardiac demand, and moderate RHD needs specialist planning, including place of birth. Missed benzathine doses should be restarted. Feeling well does not downgrade the risk, and a 3-year-old echo is not current.

A. Routine shared care is enough because she feels well
Symptoms lag behind risk.

B. Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy
Secondary prophylaxis continues in pregnancy.

E. Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis
Both the heart and the missed doses need action.

C. Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive
Place of birth is a specialist decision.

D. RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago
Three years is not a current assessment.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Moderate RHD in pregnancy needs specialist care and continuous benzathine prophylaxis. Feeling well is not the clearance.
key_takeaways: Pregnancy is a high-risk setting for RHD.
Secondary prophylaxis continues.
